title: Types of Data in Medical Research — Test

mcqs.q: Data are defined as:
opts: Recorded observations, measurements, or information collected during a research study for analysis and interpretation
The conclusions drawn at the end of a study
The statistical tests applied to a sample
The variables listed in the research protocol
mcqs.explain: In the hypertension scenario, age, sex, blood pressure, smoking status, BMI and family history are all data.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among what data allow researchers to do?
opts: Describe health conditions and identify disease patterns
Test research hypotheses and evaluate treatments
mcqs.explain: Data enable analysis; they do not guarantee any particular result.

mcqs.q: A variable is:
opts: A characteristic or measurement that can take different values among individuals or observations
Any number entered into statistical software
The outcome of a statistical test
A category that stays the same across the sample
mcqs.explain: A characteristic that cannot vary within the study is a constant, not a variable.

mcqs.q: Qualitative (categorical) data describe:
opts: Characteristics or categories rather than numerical measurements
mcqs.explain: Examples are gender, blood group, disease status, smoking status and severity of pain.

mcqs.q: Nominal data are:
opts: Categories with no natural order or ranking
mcqs.explain: Examples are blood group A, B, AB, O; sex; and diabetic versus non-diabetic.

mcqs.q: Blood group (A, B, AB, O) is an example of:
mcqs.explain: The categories are different but not ranked.

mcqs.q: If Male is coded 1 and Female is coded 2, then:
opts: The number 2 is not scientifically greater than 1 — the digits are labels, not quantities
Female participants score higher than male participants
A mean can now be calculated for sex
mcqs.explain: Numbers may be assigned as codes to nominal data but have no mathematical meaning.

mcqs.q: Which set of methods is appropriate for NOMINAL data?
opts: Frequency, percentage, mode and chi-square test
mcqs.explain: Because the categories have no order, the mode is the only meaningful average.

mcqs.q: Ordinal data are:
opts: Categories with a meaningful order or ranking
mcqs.explain: Examples are pain severity (mild, moderate, severe) and cancer stages I to IV.

mcqs.q: Cancer stage (I, II, III, IV) is an example of:
mcqs.explain: The categories have an order, but the difference between them may not be equal.

mcqs.q: The key limitation of ordinal data is that:
opts: The difference between categories may not be equal
They cannot be presented in a table
mcqs.explain: The step from mild to moderate may not equal the step from moderate to severe.

mcqs.q: Which set of methods is appropriate for ORDINAL data?
mcqs.explain: The presence of order is what makes the median meaningful.

mcqs.q: Quantitative (numerical) data are:
opts: Data expressed as numbers representing measurements or counts
Data that must be normally distributed
Data collected only in experimental studies
mcqs.explain: Examples include age, weight, height, blood glucose, heart rate, number of missed teeth, number of admissions and family size.

mcqs.q: Discrete data are:
opts: Numerical data obtained by counting, usually whole numbers with no decimal values
mcqs.explain: Examples are the number of children, hospital visits, seizures or medications taken.

mcqs.q: Number of hospital admissions (0, 1, 2, 3, 4…) is an example of:
mcqs.explain: It is obtained by counting and cannot take decimal values.

mcqs.q: Continuous data are:
opts: Numerical data obtained by measurement that can take any value within a range
Coded categories with no mathematical meaning
mcqs.explain: Examples are height, weight, blood pressure, temperature and serum cholesterol.

mcqs.q: Body weight recorded as 65 kg, 65.5 kg, 65.75 kg illustrates:
mcqs.explain: A more precise instrument would give another decimal place, which is the test for continuity.

mcqs.q: The simplest rule for telling discrete from continuous data is:
opts: Counting gives discrete data; measuring gives continuous data
Anything with a unit is discrete
mcqs.explain: Discrete data are obtained by counting and continuous data by measurement.

mcqs.q: The independent variable is:
opts: The variable that is changed, compared, or considered as a possible cause
A third variable affecting the relationship
mcqs.explain: In a study of the effect of exercise on blood pressure, the exercise program is the independent variable.

mcqs.q: The dependent variable is:
opts: The variable considered as a possible cause
mcqs.explain: In the exercise study, blood pressure reduction is the dependent variable.

mcqs.q: A confounding variable is:
opts: A third variable that affects the relationship between the independent and dependent variables
A variable that is deliberately changed
mcqs.explain: In a study of coffee consumption and heart disease, possible confounders are age, smoking and physical activity.

mcqs.q: In a study of coffee consumption and heart disease, smoking is best described as a:
mcqs.explain: It is linked both to coffee consumption and to heart disease risk, so it can distort the apparent association.

mcqs.q: Age, sex, education, occupation and smoking habit are examples of:
mcqs.explain: Demographic variables are characteristics describing participants.

mcqs.q: Mortality, recovery, blood pressure change and disease occurrence are examples of:
mcqs.explain: Outcome variables are measurements representing study results.

mcqs.q: Categorical data are usually summarized by:
opts: Frequency and percentage, and described with a bar chart
Mean plus or minus standard deviation
mcqs.explain: The common tests of significance are the chi-square test and Fisher's exact test.

mcqs.q: Which tests of significance are listed for CATEGORICAL data?
opts: Chi-square test and Fisher's exact test
mcqs.explain: The t-test, ANOVA and correlation tests are used for continuous data.

mcqs.q: Continuous data are usually summarized by:
opts: Mean ± standard deviation, or median, range and mode
mcqs.explain: The common tests are the t-test, ANOVA and correlation tests.

mcqs.q: Which tests are listed for CONTINUOUS data?
mcqs.explain: The type of data determines the statistical analysis method.

mcqs.q: The best presentation for CONTINUOUS data is:
mcqs.explain: Nominal, ordinal and discrete data all suit a frequency table and bar chart.

mcqs.q: Which data types are best presented with a frequency table and bar chart?
mcqs.explain: Only continuous data form an unbroken scale, which is what a histogram requires.

mcqs.q: Coding blood groups as A = 1, B = 2, O = 3 and then analysing them as quantities is:
opts: Error 2 — using the mean for nominal data
mcqs.explain: These numbers do not represent quantity.

mcqs.q: Calculating the average blood group in a sample is:
opts: Error 2 — using the mean for nominal data, which has no meaning
A valid summary of a nominal variable
Acceptable if the sample is large
The correct way to report blood group distribution
mcqs.explain: Nominal data are summarized by frequency, percentage and mode.

mcqs.q: Error 3, ignoring data distribution, means failing to check continuous data for:
mcqs.explain: The distribution determines whether mean ± SD or median and range is the better summary.

mcqs.q: In a positively skewed distribution:
opts: Mode < median < mean, because the long right tail pulls the mean up
The mode lies to the right of the mean
mcqs.explain: In a symmetrical distribution the mean, median and mode coincide.

mcqs.q: In a perfectly symmetrical (normal) distribution:
opts: The median lies outside the range
mcqs.explain: Skew is what separates the three measures of central tendency.

mcqs.q: In a negatively skewed distribution:
opts: Mean < median < mode, because the long left tail pulls the mean down
The mean is unaffected by the tail
mcqs.explain: The mean is the measure most sensitive to extreme values.

mcqs.q: For markedly skewed continuous data, the better summary is:
mcqs.explain: This is why the distribution is checked before the summary measure is chosen.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of data type and analysis is CORRECT?
mcqs.explain: Classify the variable first, and the correct test follows from the classification.

mcqs.q: Pain severity recorded as mild, moderate or severe should be summarized with the:
mcqs.explain: It is ordinal data, and the unequal spacing between categories makes a mean misleading.

mcqs.q: Which variable in the study “Effect of exercise on blood pressure” is the dependent variable?
mcqs.explain: The exercise program is the independent variable and age would be a demographic variable or potential confounder.

saqs.q: Define data and a variable, and explain the importance of data in medical research.
saqs.a: Data are recorded observations, measurements, or information collected during a research study for analysis and interpretation. For example, in a study of risk factors associated with hypertension among adults, the data collected may include age, sex, blood pressure, smoking status, body mass index and family history of hypertension. A variable is a characteristic or measurement that can take different values among individuals or observations, for example age with values of 20, 35 or 60 years, gender as male or female, blood pressure as 120/80 mmHg, and disease status as present or absent. Data allow researchers to describe health conditions, identify disease patterns, test research hypotheses, evaluate treatments, and make evidence-based decisions.

saqs.q: Differentiate between qualitative and quantitative data, and describe their subtypes.
saqs.a: Qualitative or categorical data describe characteristics or categories rather than numerical measurements; examples in medicine are gender, blood group, disease status, smoking status and severity of pain. They are of two types. Nominal data are categories with no natural order or ranking, such as blood group A, B, AB and O; sex as male or female; and disease status as diabetic or non-diabetic; the categories are different but not ranked, and numbers may be assigned as codes but have no mathematical meaning, so coding male as 1 and female as 2 does not make 2 scientifically greater than 1. Ordinal data are categories with a meaningful order or ranking, such as pain severity as mild, moderate or severe, and cancer stage I to IV; the categories have an order but the difference between them may not be equal, so the difference between mild and moderate may not equal that between moderate and severe. Quantitative or numerical data are data expressed as numbers representing measurements or counts, such as age, weight, height, blood glucose, heart rate, number of missed teeth, number of admissions and family size. They are also of two types. Discrete data are numerical data obtained by counting; they are usually whole numbers and cannot have decimal values, such as the number of children, hospital visits, seizures or medications taken, or admissions of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. Continuous data are numerical data obtained by measurement and can take any value within a range, such as height, weight, blood pressure, temperature and serum cholesterol; for example body weight of 65 kg, 65.5 kg or 65.75 kg.

saqs.q: State the statistical methods appropriate to nominal and to ordinal data, and explain why they differ.
saqs.a: Nominal data are analysed with frequency, percentage, mode and the chi-square test. Ordinal data are analysed with the median, percentiles and rank-based tests. They differ because nominal categories have no order, so there is nothing to take a median or mean of and the mode, the most frequent category, is the only meaningful average; ordinal categories do have an order, which is what makes the median and percentiles meaningful, but because the difference between categories may not be equal a mean would still be misleading.

saqs.q: Identify and define the types of variables in medical research, with examples.
saqs.a: The independent variable is the variable that is changed, compared, or considered as a possible cause; in a study on the effect of exercise on blood pressure, the independent variable is the exercise program. The dependent variable is the outcome being measured; in the same study it is blood pressure reduction. A confounding variable is a third variable that affects the relationship between the independent and dependent variables; in a study of coffee consumption and heart disease, possible confounders are age, smoking and physical activity. Demographic variables are characteristics describing participants, such as age, sex, education, occupation and smoking habit. Outcome variables are measurements representing study results, such as mortality, recovery, blood pressure change and disease occurrence.

saqs.q: Explain how the type of data determines its summary, presentation and statistical analysis.
saqs.a: Categorical data are usually summarized by frequency and percentage, and a bar chart is used to describe them; the common tests of significance are the chi-square test and Fisher's exact test. Continuous data are usually summarized by mean plus or minus standard deviation, or by median, range and mode; the common tests are the t-test, ANOVA and correlation tests. For presentation, nominal data suit a frequency table and bar chart, ordinal data suit a frequency table and bar chart, discrete data suit a frequency table and bar chart, and continuous data suit a histogram, box plot and mean plus or minus standard deviation.

saqs.q: Describe the common errors in classifying data and why distribution matters.
saqs.a: Error one is treating categories as numbers: if blood groups are coded A equals 1, B equals 2 and O equals 3, these numbers do not represent quantity. Error two is using the mean for nominal data: calculating the average blood group has no meaning. Error three is ignoring data distribution: continuous data may require checking for normal distribution and for outliers. Distribution matters because in a positively skewed distribution the mode is less than the median which is less than the mean, since the long right tail pulls the mean up; in a symmetrical distribution the mean, median and mode coincide; and in a negatively skewed distribution the mean is less than the median which is less than the mode. As a result, for markedly skewed continuous data the median and range describe the centre far better than the mean plus or minus standard deviation, which is why the distribution must be checked before the summary measure is chosen.
